To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we introduce a physically-based forward model that allows to render time-resolved indirect light transport in a highly efficient manner and that we show how to combine this forward model with an optimization framework in order to reconstruct object geometry from non-line-of-sight measurements.

(i) we introduce a novel algorithm that is the first to combine a physically-based renderer with an optimization framework for non-line-of-sight (NLOS) reconstruction, (ii) we demonstrate that the resulting algorithm produces physically plausible reconstructions that are more consistent with real-world data than previous work, and (iii) we show that our algorithm is more efficient than existing approaches, and can handle uncooperative scenes and non-diffuse materials.

(1) the proposed method produces reconstructions of shape and reflectance that are consistent with physically based rendering; and (2) the proposed method is efficient, robust, and produces high quality results.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions.

the problem of reconstructing the geometry and reflectance properties from a time-resolved indirect light measurement, and we demonstrate that our approach is able to produce accurate and physically-based reconstructions.
a novel approach to reconstruct geometry of objects that are occluded by a wall or other opaque surface, using time-resolved measurements.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we present a new algorithm for reconstructing shape from non-line-of-sight measurements.
the proposed method is a promising candidate for non-line-of-sight (NLOS) reconstruction, and that it is capable of producing physically-plausible results.

we present a novel reconstruction scheme for NLOS imaging that, by design and in practice, produces solutions that agree well with physically-based rendering, while being robust to noise, non-diffuse reflectance, and uncooperative scenes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are able to reconstruct a scene that is hidden around a corner, from time-resolved measurements, with physically plausible solutions, using an analysis-by-sythesis approach, in a few seconds.
we present an efficient and accurate method to reconstruct shape and reflectance from time-resolved measurements.
we have developed a novel reconstruction algorithm that can produce high quality results in challenging scenes with a wide variety of material and geometry.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, by leveraging the power of modern graphics hardware, it is now possible to efficiently solve for the inverse problem of time-resolved non-line-of-sight imaging.
the rendering community can now use time-resolved measurements to validate and improve their rendering algorithms, and that the rendering community has a novel application to explore.
, by using a physically-based renderer as a forward model, we are able to produce solutions that are consistent not only with the data, but also with physically plausible solutions.
